title: Sole Meunière
subtitle: Sole fried in butter with lemon and parsley
excerpt: Whole sole or fillets dusted in flour and fried in foaming butter until golden, then served with a quick brown butter sauce sharpened with lemon. The dish that converted Julia Child to French cooking on her first day in France.
sourceNotes: Sole meunière is one of the simplest and most celebrated of French fish dishes. Julia Child documented her first taste of it at La Couronne in Rouen in 1948 as the meal that launched her passion for French cooking, describing it in My Life in France (2006). Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), establishes the method. The word meunière means 'miller's wife', the flour dusting recalls the miller's trade.

glossaryTerms.definition: Brown butter. Butter melted and cooked until the milk solids turn golden and the butter smells of hazelnuts (noisette). It is the fast finish sauce for sole meunière and many other French fish and vegetable dishes. The moment it turns the correct amber colour it must come off the heat, as the transition from perfect to burnt takes seconds.

content.text: Sole meunière is flour, butter, lemon, and parsley, one of the most minimal compositions in French cooking, and one that depends entirely on the quality of the fish and the care taken with the butter. The fish cooks in foaming butter in 3 to 4 minutes per side, then the butter in the pan continues over the heat until it turns nut-brown,
, before being poured over the fish with lemon juice. The whole process takes 10 minutes.

items.prepNote: or 2 small whole sole, skinned; about 120 g each fillet
divided: 30 g for frying, 50 g for the beurre noisette

content.text: Pat the sole fillets thoroughly dry. Season with salt and pepper. Dust both sides in the seasoned flour and shake off the excess. The flour coating should be thin and even.

Melt 30 g of the butter in the frying pan over medium-high heat until the foam subsides. Add the sole fillets presentation-side down and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until golden. Turn carefully with a flat spatula and cook for 2 to 3 minutes more. Transfer to warm plates.

Add the remaining 50 g of butter to the pan. Cook over medium heat, swirling the pan, watching carefully. Within 1 to 2 minutes the butter will foam, the foam will subside, and the milk solids will begin to turn golden brown. The moment it smells of hazelnuts and the colour is a deep golden amber, remove from the heat immediately and add the lemon juice, it will spit. Add the parsley, swirl, and pour directly over the fish. Serve with lemon wedges.

items.symptom: The butter burnt before turning golden
items.cause: The heat was too high, or the process was not watched closely enough.
items.fix: Beurre noisette and beurre noir (black butter) are separated by a matter of seconds. Have the lemon juice ready in advance and remove from the heat the moment the colour is right. The residual heat in the pan will continue to cook the butter after removal.

items.symptom: The fish broke apart when turning
items.cause: Sole fillets are very delicate and the flour coating had not fully adhered.
items.fix: Use a flat fish spatula and slide under the full length of the fillet in one motion. Pat very dry before flouring; wet fish makes the flour paste rather than adhering as a light crust.

items.cause: Too much flour, or the fish was not dried before coating.
items.fix: Pat the fillets completely dry. Dust in flour and shake firmly in both hands to remove every possible excess. The coating should be a barely-visible film, not a layer.

content.text: Sole meunière is one of the most recognised French fish dishes. It appears on brasserie and restaurant menus across the country. Julia Child wrote about her first taste of it at a restaurant in Rouen in 1948, describing it as a turning point in how she understood food. The dish established its hold on the French and later English-speaking repertoire partly through that account in her memoir My Life in France. Dover sole is caught in the English Channel and the Bay of Biscay and has been a feature of French coastal cooking for centuries.
